title: What Type of Women Can Become Pregnant and Who to Train with Them? Differences Between Sedentary, Active, and Athlete Women
summary:
The chapter describes three profiles of pregnant women (sedentary, active and athlete) and explains that prior activity level shapes how pregnancy adaptations occur. It defines each profile and notes that only 23% of pregnant women report meeting recommended activity guidelines, with lower rates in overweight or obese women.

Sedentary women tend to have more weight gain, more risk of gestational diabetes and hypertension, and higher anxiety and depression, so they should start gently with low-impact activity. Active women can usually continue their routine at moderate intensity. Athletes can keep training but must adjust intensity, duration and type. All need prior medical evaluation, gradual change and monitoring. The chapter warns that women who train several times a week may still be sedentary the rest of the day, and that every program must be personalized.
points: Only 23% of pregnant women report meeting recommended physical activity guidelines, and the figure is lower for overweight or obese women.
Pregnant women spend more than 50% of their time in sedentary behaviors, defined as waking behavior at 1.5 METs or less while sitting, reclining or lying.
A sedentary person does little or no activity, an active person meets international recommendations, and an athlete trains intensely and in a structured way to improve performance.
Sedentary women show lower muscle tone, higher body fat, lower aerobic capacity, more pronounced weight gain and more risk of gestational diabetes and hypertension.
Sedentary women should start with walking, swimming or prenatal yoga and accumulate at least 150 minutes of moderate activity per week across several days.
Muscle-strengthening should be done twice a week for sedentary women, focusing on the core and pelvic floor.
Active women can continue their usual routine without medical contraindications, at moderate intensity, avoiding high-impact or fall-risk exercise.
Athletes can continue training but should avoid high-impact exercise, fall-risk activities and positions that may compromise blood flow.
All women need prior medical evaluation, gradual adaptation, constant monitoring, and education and support.
takeaways: Get a complete medical evaluation before starting or continuing an exercise program.
Change the routine gradually from your current fitness level.
Beginners should begin with short sessions of walking, swimming or prenatal yoga and build duration and intensity slowly.
Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus strength work twice a week.
Active women and athletes should listen to the body, prioritize recovery, and watch for excessive fatigue, pain or discomfort.
Reduce sitting time all day, even if you train three times a week.
cautions: A complete medical evaluation is essential before any pregnancy exercise program to identify contraindications.
Avoid high-impact exercises and activities with a risk of falling.
Athletes should avoid exercise positions that may compromise blood flow.
